deep_why: The system must balance inference speed and accuracy by deciding which requests run on the device versus the cloud. It does this by training a small on-device model with task-specific parameter refinements that preserve the understanding of how images and text interact, while a fast scheduler predicts which tasks need the cloud's larger model. This works because the small model learns shared cross-modal patterns once, and then only adjusts a tiny fraction of its parameters per task, reducing memory without destroying the alignment that makes vision and language work together. By routing simple, frequent requests locally and complex requests to the cloud, the system cuts costs and latency while a learned scheduler ensures the right requests reach the right tier.

The core task is finding the best configuration settings for an inference engine across different hardware by testing many combinations efficiently. The method uses a mathematical search strategy that learns which settings matter most by examining prior trials, then proposes promising new candidates rather than trying everything blindly. This works because each trial gives feedback about what helps throughput, and this feedback is used to build a model of which settings regions are worth exploring next, avoiding wasteful random guessing. By running many trials in parallel across machines, the search completes quickly while the model-guided strategy ensures no obviously bad configurations are suggested, thus exposing performance gains that default settings miss.

The task is determining whether an image shows a prepubescent, pubescent, or adult individual by combining three independent visual cues: facial features, body proportions, and anatomical characteristics. This fusion works because each source captures a different dimension of development—faces change gradually, bodies grow at specific rates, and anatomical markers are cumulative—so together they provide overlapping but distinct evidence that reduces misclassification. The system mimics human expert reasoning, which also considers multiple criteria in concert rather than any single measurement. By integrating these three signals, the classifier becomes both more interpretable (experts understand why each cue matters) and more robust, as an attacker would need to fool all three sources simultaneously rather than exploiting a single weak spot.

The core challenge is optimizing spending in marketing when the budget itself depends on whether campaigns succeed: if spending works, revenue grows and more budget becomes available; if it fails, budget shrinks. The system uses a dual optimization approach that manages this feedback loop by separating the decision-making into two coordinated parts: one controlling immediate spending, the other managing the long-term reinvestment rate. This works because the mathematical structure ensures the two parts stay consistent even as the budget changes, preventing spirals where bad feedback collapses the system. By protecting against ruin through risk-aware decisions, the method lets marketers invest when conditions improve without catastrophic loss when conditions worsen, and learns the optimal reinvestment fraction by trial.

The task is predicting when a user will make their next purchase by feeding previous purchase timing information to a language model. The finding is that adding many details about the user actually hurts prediction accuracy, contrary to intuition. This happens because the model was trained primarily on text, not numerical timing patterns; it excels at understanding semantic meaning but struggles to extract quantitative regularities from sequences of dates. When given more context, the model gets distracted by linguistic relationships rather than focusing on the temporal intervals themselves. The result reveals that language models lack the built-in mathematical machinery to capture time as a quantity the way specialized statistical methods do, so too much context introduces noise rather than signal.

The task is predicting what a user will like next by tracking how their preferences change over time. The key insight is that simply updating the user's representation with each new action overwrites past patterns, so the system loses sight of how preferences evolved. The method solves this by storing a full history of how representations looked at each previous interaction time, then selectively restoring older versions when making recommendations. This works because user preferences follow temporal structure—a user who bought A then B then C at specific times teaches us something different than one who did it in reverse, and that sequence matters. By retracing the historical path and letting the model consider what the user looked like at each decision point in their past, recommendations become calibrated to actual preference evolution rather than just the latest snapshot.

The task is training a smaller student model to understand complex graph structures with high-order relationships by learning from multiple larger teacher models. Using multiple teachers works because different teachers may have learned different aspects of the graph structure—one might excel at capturing certain node relationships, another at hyperedge patterns—so combining their knowledge gives the student richer information than any single teacher. This works because graph relationships are inherently diverse; no single expert perspective captures them fully. By having the student also learn a contrasting loss that separates different structures rather than purely imitating outputs, it builds its own discriminative ability rather than merely compressing teacher predictions, allowing it to even outperform the teachers by combining insights that none had fully mastered.

This is a workshop summary on analyzing multimodal social media content (text, images, audio, video) with large models. The core challenge being addressed is that social media combines multiple media types and languages, spreading harmful content across platforms, requiring methods that fuse information from different modalities and handle real-world deployment risks. The mathematical principle is that fusing multimodal signals increases signal-to-noise ratio for content detection because harmful content often correlates across modalities—words and images aligned, tones matching—making it detectable through cross-modal consistency. The workshop focuses on developing models robust to hallucinations and adversarial attacks, recognizing that safety depends not just on raw accuracy but on controlling failure modes in deployed systems.

The task is selecting which retrieved documents to rank highest when using a language model to answer questions with external sources. Standard reranking algorithms push factually correct documents higher, improving accuracy, but inadvertently also elevate harmful false documents. The method balances accuracy gains against the risk that misleading documents will steer the language model toward generating false or misleading answers. This works because the gain from correct documents can be measured independently from the risk of incorrect ones; rather than maximizing accuracy alone, the system chooses a threshold that trades off these objectives. By explicitly measuring both benefits and harms of each reranking decision, the system prevents scenarios where improved recall of good documents is outweighed by amplified risk of bad documents corrupting the final generation.

The task is inferring which websites and specific subpages a user visits by analyzing network traffic patterns without looking at encrypted content. The system frames this as a hierarchical classification problem: first identify which website, then which subpage within it. This works because traffic patterns differ across websites and again across pages within a site, and these differences follow a nested structure—a subpage pattern is constrained by being part of a specific website. The model uses cross-attention to capture how homepage traffic patterns relate to subpage patterns, then enforces hierarchy constraints to prevent impossible predictions. By modeling the multi-level dependencies explicitly rather than treating each possibility independently, the system exploits the natural structure of how users browse to achieve finer-grained accuracy.

The task is detecting unusual points in streaming time series data where the data distribution shifts over time and memory is limited. The method builds a small, compressed summary of historical data called a proxy that captures what normal looked like, then updates this proxy as new data arrives. This works because a good proxy prevents the need to store all past examples; instead, a single compact representation can stand in for millions of historical points when checking whether new data matches the expected pattern. The system adds a multi-level feature extraction that explicitly captures correlations at different time scales, recognizing that anomalies manifest differently—some as local spikes, others as trend shifts. By combining an efficient evolving proxy with selective parameter activation, the system detects drifting anomalies without exceeding memory or compute budgets.

This is a workshop summary on harmful content diffusion (misinformation, hate speech, cyber-bullying) across platforms, languages, and media types, particularly in the age of large language models and autonomous agents. The core challenge is that harmful content spreads across multiple channels—social media, news, comments, links—in multiple languages, and blocking or removing it can simply drive spreaders to different platforms. The mathematical principle underlying detection is that harmful content, while diverse in form, correlates with linguistic markers and user behavior patterns that can be learned. The workshop emphasizes studying these phenomena holistically across platforms and languages rather than in isolation, recognizing that understanding diffusion mechanisms requires seeing the full ecosystem picture.

The task is aggregating information from neighbors in a network graph where not all neighbors share the same labels or features as their connections. Standard approaches assume neighbors are similar, but this breaks when the graph contains many dissimilar connections. The method uses a geometric measure called Ricci curvature—which describes how space curves and bends—to weight the influence of each neighbor's information based on how similar that connection actually is. This works because curvature naturally captures whether two connected nodes occupy similar regions of the graph; high curvature means the connection is meaningful and bending, low curvature means nodes are truly aligned. By using this geometric principle alongside node features and network structure, the method can aggregate information intelligently even when many edges violate the similarity assumption.

The task is forecasting future values in multivariate time series by extracting meaningful patterns from frequency-domain information. The method separates high-amplitude periodic patterns from low-amplitude signals, because these require different handling: high-amplitude patterns convey strong predictive signals but neural transformations can distort them, while low-amplitude signals get buried by noise in standard training. By using temporal geometry to identify which low-amplitude details matter and processing high-frequency information separately through attention to preserve periodicity, the system recovers signals that single-path models miss. The final aggregation uses residual connections to combine both streams, ensuring neither dominates; this works because many forecasting problems involve both strong oscillations and subtle trend information that require different extraction strategies.

The task is computing low-dimensional embeddings of users distributed across multiple organizations such that the computation is mathematically proven secure and never reveals individual data. The method adapts a classical manifold learning technique using secret sharing, where each organization holds shares of the data that are individually meaningless but collectively encode the true answer. This works because secret sharing guarantees that no subset of participants (including the system itself) can reconstruct private data from the shares—security is mathematical, not policy-based. The optimization focuses on the two most expensive operations—finding nearest neighbors and computing shortest paths—introducing secure protocols that replace naive methods with algorithms exploiting the specific structure of these problems, drastically reducing communication without breaking privacy.
